item.title: Big cities can make money, but they turn couples into long-distance relationships
item.description:
Big cities offer opportunities to make money, while hometowns do not. The starting point for many couples living apart is not a problem with their relationship, but rather the reality both face: income opportunities are concentrated in big cities, and they want to stay together, yet they lack sufficient housing and financial breathing room.

When we were in school, our imagination of the future was often simple: leave work on time, go home and learn something we’re interested in, and go out for a walk on weekends. Few people imagined that later they wouldn’t be able to afford a house, would have to work overtime every day, or would even be too lazy to move after coming home from work or on weekends. When making money and living must be chosen between, marriage is easily arranged into two cities first.

Making money opportunities on one side, life needs on the other side

“Big cities make money, hometowns don’t” is not true for everyone, but it is enough to illustrate the dilemma of a certain type of ordinary people. Hometowns have familiar people and life, while big cities offer more job opportunities; one place is better suited for settling down, while the other is easier to make money in. When two people want both at the same time, they often have to pay a price beyond what their family can afford.

Thus, the choices will gradually become several arrangements that are none of them easy:

  • Two people return to their hometown. Living closer together, but income and career choices may shrink.
  • Both stay in a big city. Work opportunities remain in the same place, yet housing and daily costs become a higher threshold.
  • One stays in the big city, the other stays in the hometown. At least one side keeps their income, and the other keeps a relatively familiar life. Distance becomes the easiest compromise to execute.

This is not about who values their career more or who is less willing to compromise. In many cases, a couple simply splits the family apart to shoulder different costs separately: one bears the pressure of earning money, while the other bears the pressure of staying put. The marriage still exists, and so does the family — only the shared life has been postponed.

After Not Being Able to Afford a House, What Marriage Loses First Is the Everyday

A house was originally a container for shared life. When it becomes unaffordable, it stops being just a housing issue and becomes a question of who stays, who compromises, and who bears the cost.

This is also why long-distance couples are usually the first to lose not some major holiday, but those everyday moments that don’t require advance planning: having dinner together, chatting a bit after work, or spontaneously going out for a stroll on the weekend. Each person lives in their own city, meeting up requires arrangement, relocating means recalculating jobs and income, and even ordinary companionship becomes something that needs to be coordinated.

The life one desires while reading is not extravagant. Leaving work on time, doing something that interests you a little, going out for a walk on weekends—these all seem small, yet they are precisely what it means for two people to truly live together. When these small things are continually kept out by housing and income, marriage is left with nothing but scheduled meetings and obligations that need to be fulfilled.

Overtime Consumes More Than Just Time After Work

Distance can still be bridged through meeting in person, but exhaustion can hardly be resolved by simply saying “communicate more.”

People who work overtime every day just want to lie down when they get home; when the weekend finally arrives with some free time, they can no longer be bothered to move. It’s not that they don’t want to talk—it’s that they’ve already used up all their energy for the day; it’s not that they don’t want to meet up—it’s that they have to talk themselves into even stepping out the door. For couples living in different cities, communication, travel, and maintaining the relationship all require extra time, and work happens to chip away at that time bit by bit.

A relationship rarely cools down in a single evening. More often, it gradually loses its original shape after countless instances of “see you next week,” after too many nights without the energy to talk, after putting off what should have been said to some later time. Both people know life is hard, and both are trying to keep their own side of it going. But what shared life actually requires is not that each person perseveres on their own, but that two people can share a stretch of time that hasn’t been entirely consumed by work.

So, couples living apart often don’t lack reminders to “cherish the relationship.” What they lack even more are the real conditions that allow two people to work, live, and rest at the same time. Talking only about persistence without addressing income and housing; talking only about communication without acknowledging how overtime wears people down—in the end, this just hands a practical problem back to the willpower of the two individuals.

Big cities make money, hometowns don’t. This choice has allowed many people to keep their income, but not their lives. Living apart is a distance on the map; what truly makes it hard for two people to come together is that neither has the energy left to live their lives alongside each other.

References

This article is written solely based on the user’s life observations and does not cite any external materials.

写作附记

Original Prompt

Big cities offer opportunities to make money, while hometowns don’t, which has led to many married couples living apart these days. When I was studying, I never imagined that I wouldn’t be able to afford a house, or that I’d be working overtime every day. What I thought about back then was finishing work on time, going home to learn things I was interested in, and going out on weekends. Now, on weekends I’m too lazy to move, and after work I’m too lazy to move when I get home.

item.title: China's Sports Reform Should Give Ordinary Children a Ball to Play With
item.description:
Fan Zhendong going to Germany to play has touched a familiar expectation: the country cultivates the best athletes, and they should stay on the familiar courts we know, continuing to bring home the gold medals. And with the Chinese men’s table tennis team being eliminated early in high-level events one after another, while a Japanese newcomer has already won an adult competition championship, the anxiety about succession now has real results to back it up. Chinese sports needs to explain the changes in competitiveness right before our eyes, and also answer questions beyond the national team roster: if an ordinary child likes playing table tennis, can they keep playing without betting on their education and family savings?

First, let’s clarify the matter about Fan Zhendong

The controversy surrounding Fan Zhendong has extended beyond a single season. This article discusses the relationship between his withdrawal from the world rankings, his move to play in Germany, and the talent system, based on publicly verifiable information as of September 15, 2026.

On December 31, 2024, the Chinese Table Tennis Association confirmed that Ma Long, Fan Zhendong, and Chen Meng have withdrawn from the world rankings, stating that they respect their decisions and have communicated with the International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF) and WTT regarding competition rule adjustments based on the athletes’ concerns. This statement does not equate withdrawing from the rankings with retirement, and it certainly cannot be used as a basis to announce Fan Zhendong’s withdrawal from the national team. Xinhua News Agency report on the Chinese Table Tennis Association’s statement

There has been new progress in his move to play in Germany. Borussia Düsseldorf announced a contract with him for the 2026/27 season; the club’s match report dated August 23, 2026 records that he achieved two singles victories in the team’s home match. Therefore, it is no longer accurate to summarize his German experience simply as “joining Saarbrücken.” Contract announcement, Düsseldorf home match report

In April 2025, Calderano won the men’s singles championship at the Macau World Cup; a month later, Wang Chuqin defeated him in the men’s singles final at the Doha World Table Tennis Championships to claim the title, while Sun Yingsha also won the women’s singles championship. These results show that Team China still has top players, but they do not answer the question of what happened to the overall depth and succession of the men’s team more than a year later. Macau World Cup report, Doha World Table Tennis Championships report

Dismissing all athletes because of a single defeat is too simplistic; using past championships to offset a recent string of losses would also overlook the real problems. Whether the selection is reasonable, whether the training is effective, and whether reserve players can step into the starters’ roles should all be examined through the lens of recent competitions.

Fan Zhendong’s experience is more suited to raising another set of questions: how much choice do athletes have over their competition schedules and professional lives? How do performances at overseas clubs enter the national team’s talent selection radar? For already-established athletes, how are rest periods, commercial events, and national team duties coordinated? These questions deserve open discussion. Transfers and withdrawals from rankings alone are not enough to write “being marginalized” as fact.

Consecutive Losses Have Triggered a Succession Alarm

This round of concerns is not only driven by fans’ obsession with the “must-win championship” mentality. On September 12, 2026, CCTV News reported that China’s men’s table tennis team had failed to reach the semifinals in four consecutive WTT high-level events: the U.S. Grand Smash, Yokohama Champions, Sweden Grand Smash, and Macau Champions. Failing to reach the semifinals at four events in a row is a problem of a different magnitude from occasionally losing a final. Reported by CCTV News, reposted by CNR

Spreading out the matches at both ends, the changes become clearer:

Date & Event Specific Defeat Impact on the Tournament Results
July 3, 2026, US Grand Slam Wang Chuqin lost 1–3 to Denmark’s Anders Lind; Lin Shidong lost 0–3 to France’s Alex Lebrun Both were eliminated in the Round of 16; no Chinese men’s singles players advanced to the quarterfinals
September 2026, Macao Championships, First and Second Rounds Huang Youzheng lost 2–3 to USA’s Jaha; Chen Yuanyu lost 2–3 to Slovenia’s Darko Jorgic Eliminated in the first round and Round of 16, respectively
September 12, 2026, Macao Championships Quarterfinals Zhou Qihao lost 1–4 to Japan’s Tomokazu Harimoto The last remaining Chinese men’s singles player was eliminated; no Chinese player reached the semifinals

The U.S. stop results can be found in a CCTV News report, reposted by China Youth Online; the results of the top two players at the Macau stop can be found in the aforementioned CNR report, and Zhou Qihao’s matches can be found in a Yangzi Evening News match report. What is listed here are specific external match and stage results; matches from different-level tournaments, qualifiers, and internal team encounters are not lumped together as a single “loss count.”

The Macau stop has one condition that must be stated: according to Yangzi Evening News, Wang Chuqin and Lin Shidong withdrew due to injuries, and the players who competed were Zhou Youhao, Chen Yuanyu, and Huang Youzheng. Therefore, this stop is not sufficient to gauge the ceiling of the full main lineup. However, at the U.S. stop, both Wang Chuqin and Lin Shidong participated, and no men’s singles player made it to the quarterfinals, so this round of poor performance cannot be entirely attributed to “the main players not being there.”

The absence of key players can also expose another issue: how much of the burden can the players behind them shoulder? If the team can only maintain its ability to compete for the championship or even advance to the latter stages of the tournament by relying on a very small number of players being available, the depth of the bench is worth questioning. The results across four consecutive stops are already enough to demand that the coaching staff explain the lineup, training, and match arrangements; as for how much responsibility falls on injuries, form, technical response, and selection respectively, each factor still needs to be analyzed one by one.

This also doesn’t mean that the entire Chinese table tennis team has lost competitiveness across all events. While no men’s singles player advanced to the quarterfinals at the 2026 US Grand Slam, Sun Yingsha and Kuai Man met in the women’s singles final, and the Chinese team also won the men’s doubles and women’s doubles titles. Pointing out the men’s singles issue separately allows the succession pressure to fall on specific teams and training processes. Tokyo TV Tournament Summary

Japan Has Already Made Breakthroughs, and Germany Is Also Supplementing the Next Generation

The change in Japan is evidenced by their performance in adult competitions. In January 2026, Matsushima Haruku defeated Tomokazu Harimoto in the semifinals of the All Japan Championships, then won the men’s singles final 4-0 over Daito Shinozuka, achieving back-to-back men’s singles titles. By July, he had also won the US Grand Smash final 4-2 over Sidorenko. The Japanese men’s team now has a player other than Tomokazu Harimoto who has won a WTT top-tier Grand Smash singles title. Japan Table Tennis Association All Japan Championship Report, US Grand Smash Full Results

At the same U.S. stop, Daito Shinozuka also defeated Wen Ruibo and Calderano in succession to reach the quarterfinals. The significance of this example is that the competition among Japan’s younger generation is no longer confined to domestic trials—it has already translated into results on the senior international stage. For the relevant match outcomes, see the U.S. Grand Smash record mentioned above.

The German evidence is on another level. In June 2026, the men’s singles final of the European U21 Championship was contested between Andre Bertelsmeier and Wim Verdonschot, with the former winning 4-3. Bertelsmeier’s name also appears on the German squad for the London World Table Tennis Championships as announced by the European Table Tennis Union. European U21 Final Report, German Senior Team Roster Introduction

These facts indicate that some German players have progressed from youth competitions to the adult national team, but a European youth championship cannot be directly equated with an adult world-class championship. Whether this German group can take over the international competitive position of the Boll and Ovtcharov generation will depend on their subsequent performance in adult competitions. Stating that both Japan and Germany have “already completed the succession” would exaggerate the extent that the current evidence from Germany can demonstrate.

Similarly, Fan Zhendong’s strong performance in the German Bundesliga first proves that the league can meet the demands of professional competitions for top athletes; Chinese-trained star players playing for German clubs cannot be counted as the result of Germany’s domestic youth development. It is worth observing whether local young players can get playing opportunities in such a league, and whether they can convert the experience of competing against high-level opponents into progress.

In China, the term “gap” also needs clarification regarding what it refers to. Lin Shidong, born in 2005, has already won the 2025 Singapore Grand Slam men’s singles championship, so it cannot be said that there are no young players in China reaching a high level. Lin Shidong’s date of birth and major achievements

But having one young champion does not mean a group of players has already formed who can sustainably take over. What is more worrying in the recent results is whether young players can turn a single breakthrough into a sustained winning rate against foreign opponents; whether the second tier can continue to advance in high-level tournaments when the main players are injured or absent; and whether, when facing opponents who have already beaten them, they can come up with an effective response the next time. What the Chinese men’s singles has shown is a warning sign about sustained competitiveness and the depth of its reserves. It deserves to be discussed seriously, and it points more directly to what needs to change than a simple claim that “there is no one left in the country.”

This brings the issue back to the selection mechanism. How should the national team balance immediate results with the development of new talent? How are opportunities in international matches distributed, and on what basis can those who are not selected regain visibility? What role do youth tournament results, senior international performances, and training evaluations each play in selection? If the rules and the effectiveness of player development lack verifiable explanations, the public can only speculate after every loss. Reform should enable people to assess where talent is discovered and where it is held back, rather than only showcasing the system when winning championships and asking for patience when losing.

The strength of the women’s volleyball team is real, but whether ordinary people can play the game is another matter

The most compelling aspect of the nationwide system is its ability to concentrate coaching, training, medical, and competition resources over the long term. For events that lack commercial revenue, this sustained investment is especially important; for ordinary children from selected families, public cultivation may also reduce the direct training costs borne by their families.

The historical achievements of the women’s volleyball team cannot be dismissed as “national effort making everyone mistakenly believe they are very strong.” The five consecutive championships from 1981 to 1986, as well as subsequent titles including the 2016 Rio Olympics, are genuine competitive accomplishments. National organizational support, coaching expertise, technical training, and the athletes’ dedication together formed the foundation of these victories. 40th Anniversary Retrospective: Chinese Women’s Volleyball Team’s First World Championship

The inference that needs to be corrected is the one from a national team to society as a whole: having a world champion team does not mean that most schools have stable volleyball teams, nor does it mean that an ordinary girl can find a court, a coach, and opponents of similar skill level after school.

A gold medal measures how high the very best of a small group can reach; mass sports must also answer whether the rest of the people have a chance to participate. The two can support each other, yet one cannot be used to submit a report card in place of the other.

Similarly, being trained at a sports school and having personal interests are not mutually exclusive. Children at sports schools can genuinely enjoy sports, and children at clubs may also be pushed by their parents to practice. The question is how the system treats such interests: are children allowed to try several sports? Are they allowed to show their talent a bit later? If they don’t pursue a professional path, can they still keep up with their studies and athletic life?

For team sports like football, basketball, and volleyball, long-running leagues are especially valuable. Beyond technical skills, players must repeatedly make judgments against different opponents, rhythms, and lineups. This means that improving the talent pool requires a sufficient number of continuously operating teams and matches. Bringing the best few dozen people together can improve the quality of their training, but those who have yet to be discovered need a place to play first.

China is already changing; progress should be viewed in layers

If we continue to describe youth sports in China as having only the path of sports schools, we will miss the changes that have already taken place.

The 2020 Ti-Jiao Ronghe (Sports-Education Integration) Opinions proposed establishing school representative teams, supporting social forces to enter campuses, and connecting competitions from primary schools to universities, and from county-level to national-level. This indicates that policy direction has already recognized that learning and training need to be arranged within the same growth process. Ti-Jiao Ronghe Opinions

But policy direction, event implementation, and actual benefits for families are three different stages.

Dimension Verifiable Progress Effects That Cannot Yet Be Confirmed
Training Entry Points Policies incorporated into schools, sports schools, and social clubs Ordinary families have affordable options everywhere
Cross-System Competitions National School and Youth Games and China Youth Football League have been launched Every ordinary participant has a stable season and sufficient playing time
Local Practice Beijing has established connections among school-level, city, and regional competitions Resource-poor counties have equivalent conditions
Training Evaluation The 2026 National Conference clearly required correcting the gold medal-first tendency Assessment, income, and promotion incentives for grassroots coaches have been adjusted accordingly

The national competitions and evaluation directions in the table come from the 2026 National Youth Sports Work Conference; the local practices come from the Beijing case released by the General Administration of Sport. They demonstrate that the reform is advancing, but do not provide a nationally unified assessment of family burden or participation retention. National Conference Report, Beijing Youth Competition and Youth Training Practice

Beijing’s example is worth examining in more concrete terms. Official materials document that the 2025 Baidui Cup had 1,369 participating teams and allowed the public to freely form teams; the North China Youth Three Major Ball Leagues adopted a home-and-away double round-robin format. This adds a layer of substantive content beyond the vague announcement of “valuing sports”: it transforms who can form teams, where they play, and how they repeatedly face each other into concrete organizational arrangements. The aforementioned figures and competition formats can be found in the previously cited Beijing practice reports.

However, after organizing a successful event, there are even more difficult everyday issues to address. Can training continue after entering middle or high school? Who pays for transportation and coaching fees for weekend competitions? After the regular team loses, will there still be a next game? If a coach nurtures many children who participate long-term but never wins an award, will that put the coach at a disadvantage in performance evaluations?

My assessment is that China is expanding entry points through schools and clubs and attempting to connect different systems; the publicly available materials are still insufficient to prove that a universally accessible, affordably manageable pathway has been established. Nor is it appropriate to assign the reform a nationwide completion rate: the number of events, talent pipelines, and the participation experience of ordinary children are not measured by the same yardstick.

What’s Worth Learning from Abroad: Multiple Opportunities and Long-Term Competitions

“Free choice of sports in elementary school, joining clubs during vacations, and being discovered by a coach or scout to advance through the ranks” describes one possible developmental pathway. However, treating it as a universal experience for all children abroad would erase the differences in region, sport, and family circumstances.

German football and American collegiate sports operate under different organizational logics.

The German Football Association’s (DFB) talent development program connects grassroots clubs with higher-level training centers and football elite schools. According to the description at the time of its current certification review, U12 to U15 players selected for training points receive an additional specialized training session per week, beyond their training at their original clubs. The significance of this arrangement is that children can first stay with their local teams while receiving extra development opportunities, before transitioning to higher levels. DFB Talent Development Introduction

There are both clubs and associations providing unified organization and quality requirements. Relying on a single scout happening to pass by is not enough to support stable talent discovery; what is needed is continuous local matches, coach observation, and cooperation between levels.

The United States cannot simply fit into the European soccer club ladder. School teams and college competitions form an important pipeline, with outside clubs also participating; entering college competition and entering professional leagues are different thresholds. The NCAA itself separately tracks the probabilities of transitioning from high school, college, and professional stages, and notes that these are only estimates. NCAA Pathway Research from High School to College and Professional Competition

From these arrangements, there are three interrelated benefits that China can truly learn from.

First, the child can participate first, then decide how far they are willing to go. There is no need to immediately interpret their interest as a future career at the beginning, so the family is more likely to allow them to try.

Second, talent can be observed repeatedly. If a child isn’t selected this time, as long as there are still competitions available, they have the opportunity to receive new evaluations through their subsequent performances. The value of multiple entry points depends on the competition opportunities after not being selected.

Third, there is a connection between schools, local clubs, and higher-level teams, so the responsibility for development does not have to rest on a single institution from start to finish. Grassroots organizations are responsible for broad participation, while professional institutions take in those suited to continue improving; whether this division of labor works depends on whether the transfer-in, transfer-out, and development compensation rules can truly function.

These are the benefits that institutional design can bring; it does not mean that every foreign club has achieved them. The fact that the German Football Association still needs to build a dedicated development network shows that beyond free participation, organization and investment from someone are also required.

The club also turns interest into an increasingly expensive bill

The most easily romanticized notion is that “as long as you love it, you can keep practicing forever.”

Hmm, let me reconsider. Actually, I think I got tripped up — let me just translate this naturally:

The thing that gets romanticized the most is the idea that “as long as you love something, you can keep practicing it forever.”

According to the Project Play parent survey conducted by the Aspen Institute in the United States, in 2024, American families with children participating in sports spent an average of $1,016 on a child’s primary sport — a 46% increase compared to 2019. This figure reflects spending among participating families and cannot be interpreted as the average across all American households, nor does it represent top-tier youth training fees. Project Play Youth Sports Spending Survey

Beyond registration, there are also equipment, travel, accommodation, and additional training. Even if registration is nominally open, who can afford long-term investment may still affect who has the opportunity to accumulate training and competition experience. The cost barrier also reminds China that the proliferation of training institutions outside of schools does not mean that public sports services have improved.

Another easily overlooked point is that the career pipeline is very narrow. According to the NCAA’s estimate for the 2024 men’s basketball draft, approximately 1% of NCAA men’s basketball players eligible for the draft were selected in the NBA Draft. This percentage does not account for all other professional paths, and cannot be used to assert that the rest are unable to play professional basketball; but even those who have already entered the collegiate competition system are far from all being able to enter the top league. NCAA Estimate and Methodology

Therefore, if parents treat long-term training as an investment in scholarships or professional income, and clubs only keep selling the hope of “going one step further,” an interest may turn into another competition. Whether commercial institutions exaggerate prospects and whether they guarantee cultural learning still requires oversight.

The selection process itself does not automatically become fair simply because it is handed over to clubs. If coaches are primarily held accountable for wins and losses in the current season, they may favor children who currently have a physical advantage and can win games right away. This is a bias that short-term evaluation can produce, and it applies to any organizational structure; having multiple institutions coexist only provides conditions for error correction, and still requires reasonable grouping, development assessment, and transfer opportunities.

Therefore, social development requires public support. Low-cost venues, volunteer coaching staff, subsidies for families in difficulty, and ordinary leagues that non-selectees can still participate in — these determine whether the right to choose belongs to the majority of children, or only to families with money and time to shuttle them to and from activities.

In the End, Reform Must Reach a Child’s Saturday

The challenge for the next step of Chinese sports lies in making public investment, school education, and professional training each assume clear responsibilities.

First, schools need to provide stable conditions for most children to participate. Beyond school teams competing for rankings, class-level competitions, regular teams, and beginner training should also have people organizing them. If funding only follows the few award-winning teams, the new school sports programs may still grow into a scaled-down version of a gold medal project.

Professional development requires more transparent pathways. The eligibility criteria for registration, observation periods, selection rationale, and appeal procedures should be understandable to athletes and their families. For football, basketball, and volleyball, there should be continuous observation of young players’ actual playing time in high-quality matches, rather than merely counting those selected for rosters or short-term training camps. When mature athletes like Fan Zhendong compete overseas, how their performances are evaluated should also fall within the scope that regulations should clarify.

The professional capabilities accumulated by sports schools can continue to serve a purpose: supporting the training of grassroots coaches, providing specialized guidance to schools, and accepting children who are willing to undergo in-depth training. At the same time, the pathways for switching programs, exiting professional training, and returning to general education need to be thoughtfully arranged. The more controllable the cost of failure in training, the more willing families will be to let their children start.

To measure reform, we can first announce a few simple but useful results:

  • How many matches does an average participant actually play in a year, and how much playing time do they get.
  • What proportion of children continue to participate in sports after entering middle and high school.
  • How much does a family actually pay in a season, and what support do families in difficulty receive.
  • Among children not selected for the professional development pathway, how many continue their education and continue playing.

These metrics won’t immediately translate into a gold medal, but they can tell us whether sports has become part of everyday life.

A child should be able to walk into a nearby field on Saturday, find a team and coaches, lose the game, and still have another match the following week; years later, even if it turns out they’re not suited for a professional path, they can continue their education normally and still be willing to play with friends. Only when such experiences become commonplace can China’s sports reform be said to have truly reached ordinary people.

References

All sources below were verified on September 15, 2026; the 2026 summer tournament is used to analyze recent men’s singles performance, and the 2025 results are used to illustrate the heights the player has reached; overall win rate is not calculated based on scattered cross-year match results.

  1. Xinhua News Agency: Chinese Table Tennis Association Confirms Three Players Withdraw from World Rankings, December 31, 2024.

  2. Düsseldorf: Fan Zhendong Signing Announcement; Home Match Report on August 23, 2026.

  3. Titan Sports Weekly: Calderano Wins Macau World Cup; Chinese Olympic Committee: 2025 Doha World Table Tennis Championships Singles Results.

  4. General Administration of Sport of China: 40th Anniversary Review of Chinese Women’s Volleyball Team’s First World Championship.

  5. General Administration of Sport and Ministry of Education: 2020 Opinion on Sports-Education Integration.

  6. 2026 National Youth Sports Work Conference; Beijing Youth Competitions and Youth Training Practice.

  7. German Football Association: Talentförderung.

  8. Project Play: Family Youth Sports Spending Survey.

  9. NCAA: Probability of Competing in College Athletics Beyond High School and Estimation Methods.

  10. CCTV News: Chinese national table tennis team fails to reach men’s singles quarterfinals at 2026 US Grand Smash; Fails to reach semifinals at four consecutive events through Macau.

  11. Yangtze Evening News: Zhou Qihao loses to Tomokazu Harimoto and Macau roster.

  12. Japan Table Tennis Association: Harimoto Tomokazu clinches second consecutive All-Japan men’s singles title; Butterfly Table Tennis Report: Complete results of 2026 US Grand Smash men’s singles; TV Tokyo tournament summary.

  13. European Table Tennis Union: German players meet in the final of 2026 U21 men’s singles; Germany’s adult national team and national championship roster.

  14. Lin Shidong: Date of birth and major achievements.

写作附记

Original Prompt

$blog-writer In China, many sports operate under a state-run system rather than being driven by personal interest, especially in light of the recent Fan Zhendong incident. Previously, people in China believed that table tennis was an invincible discipline for us—as long as we competed, we would win gold medals. Now things have changed: the key players we’ve cultivated have left, those who remain lack sufficient ability, and issues have emerged in the selection mechanism. This doesn’t even mention football, basketball, or volleyball. The former glory of the Chinese women’s volleyball team was also a product of the sports school era—mobilizing national efforts made everyone feel that the Chinese women’s volleyball team was incredibly strong. In foreign selection models, children in elementary school are free to participate in various sports, choosing what they like. During holidays, they can continue training at clubs. If coaches think they have potential, or if they’re spotted by scouts, they can advance to higher-level clubs, participate in youth professional leagues, and work their way up. Analyze the progress of China’s sports reform and the advantages and disadvantages of foreign models.

item.title: Family Planning Thinned Out Clans, But It Didn't Decide Who Could Become a Tycoon
item.description:
When you put family planning, public officials, and American plutocratic families together in the same question, it’s easy to arrive at a smooth-sounding answer: fewer children make it harder for great families to form; China has no Rockefellers, but America does, because America doesn’t strictly restrict births. This answer compresses three different problems into one.

Family planning did thin out the horizontal branches of families, especially the networks of siblings and cousins; but it alone cannot explain why a country did not develop wealth dynasties of the American kind. For a family to evolve from “many relatives” to “sustained control of wealth or power” also requires property rights, corporations, inheritance, and organizational relationships. Population policy affects how many nodes a family has; institutions determine whether those nodes hold assets that can be passed down.

Family Planning Is First and Foremost a Population Policy, Not an Anti-Family Policy

In the decades after the founding of New China, the population did indeed grow rapidly. Historical data from the National Bureau of Statistics show that the population increased from approximately 540 million in 1949 to 830 million in 1970, and reached about 960 million in 1978. Social stability, improvements in healthcare, and the decline in mortality—themselves achievements of modernization—simultaneously placed immense pressure on food supply, housing, education, employment, and fiscal expenditure. National Bureau of Statistics: Coordinating Population Development Strategy to Achieve Balanced Population Development

So, what family planning originally aimed to address was the contradiction between population growth rate and developmental capacity. In the early 1970s, the policy slogan was still “later, sparser, fewer”; in 1978, family planning was written into the constitution; in 1980, the Central Committee’s open letter required Party members, Youth League members, and especially cadres at all levels to take the lead in having only one child. The strict policy was progressively tightened along this timeline—it did not exist from the very first day the People’s Republic was founded.

This time difference is important. If “the early years after the founding of the PRC” refers to the period from 1949 to the 1960s and 1970s, then the strict family planning policies that emerged later cannot be used to explain why large clans did not appear in the earlier period. The family and political relationships of that time had already taken shape within a different demographic environment; family planning mainly affected those born after the 1980s.

We must not reverse-engineer “population control” into “blocking family power.” The stated policy goal is to slow population growth, ease resource constraints, and serve modernization. It may produce the social side effect of weakening extended families, but that is not the same as its declared institutional purpose.

Public Officials Are Strictly Governed Because Organizations Can Govern Them

Public officials are required to take the lead in having fewer children. Behind this lies a straightforward governance rationale: to demonstrate that a policy can cover all families, it must first show that members of the organization itself are bound by the same rules. The difference is that ordinary families mainly face publicity efforts, services, and local administration, while public officials are also embedded in chains of workplace authority, performance reviews, promotions, party discipline, and administrative discipline—meaning the cost of enforcement is lower and the consequences are more direct.

The Population and Family Planning Law amended in 2015 had stipulated that state employees who violated birth policies and paid social maintenance fees should also be subject to administrative sanctions according to law. Historical regulations in places such as Beijing also linked occupational opportunities such as being selected for honors, promotion, and salary advancement to violations of birth policies.Population and Family Planning Law amended in 2015Historical Versions of Beijing Population and Family Planning Regulations

Therefore, the observation that “public officials face stronger restrictions” is basically valid, but it reflects stronger organizational constraints rather than public officials being assigned a different demographic target. During the 2021 amendment, the legislative explanation explicitly mentioned the elimination of social maintenance fees, the removal of related disciplinary provisions, and the promotion of cleaning up regulations that linked individual fertility situations to school enrollment, household registration, and employment. National People’s Congress: Explanation on the Draft Amendment to the Population and Family Planning Law

This also explains why the public sector portion looks particularly “hard”: they are not only policy subjects but also organization members. Organizations are able to connect family choices to professional consequences, so enforcement is no longer merely an advocacy effort.

One Less Child and One Less Tycoon Are Not the Same Thing

If “Dazong groups” are “Dazong lineages,” then the family planning policy certainly has an impact on them.

When a family has only one child, there are fewer siblings; the number of cousins in the next generation also decreases; and there are fewer opportunities for relatives to be distributed across different cities, units, and industries. The traditional clan structure, which relied on multiple branches spreading out, will indeed become thinner. For families of cadres, the number of children who can simultaneously enter different organizational nodes is reduced, and the lateral expansion of family networks will also be limited.

But “clan”, “power family”, and “family capital” are not the same concept:

Type Mainly Relies On What Family Planning May Affect What Cannot Be Explained Alone
Lineage Number of relatives and long-term relationships Number of siblings, cousins, and branch lineages Whether wealth can be inherited across generations
Power Family Positions, political trust, and organizational networks Kinship nodes a family can spread out Who can gain sustained organizational trust
Family Capital Inheritable property rights, companies, and financial structures Number of heirs and resource allocation Whether property rights allow long-term privatization

The most confusing row in this table is the last one: having fewer children first removes relative nodes, it does not automatically erase assets, nor does it automatically change who controls the assets.

For early Chinese history, the ownership transformation of the 1950s may be a more critical variable. After the socialist transformation of private industry and commerce, the path of private enterprises continuously expanding as family property was no longer the mainstream institutional path. CPPCC: The Socialist Transformation of Capitalist Industry and Commerce

This is a completely different inheritance mechanism from a father handing over company shares, factories, mines, or a bank to his son. In early China, important resources were more attached to organizational identity, public sector positions, and political relationships, rather than to a shareholding table that could be freely traded, mortgaged, and inherited. A position could bring advantages to a family, but it did not equate to private property rights.

Family planning may even produce the opposite effect: lateral family branches become fewer, but the concentration of resources on a single heir may be higher. An only child faces the assets and caregiving responsibilities of two parents and four grandparents. It reduces the strength that comes from many siblings, but does not necessarily reduce the family resources held by one person.

Therefore, the family planning policy may weaken the size of traditional large clans, but it cannot be treated as the main explanation for why China lacks American-style wealthy families. The question is not how many children a family has, but whether the family can place its wealth into a kind of institutionally stable container that persists across generations.

Wealthy American Families Rely on the Continuity of Property Rights

“Plutocratic family” is not a strict classification in American law. When we look at several famous American families together, we can see that their formation roughly went through four steps.

The formation of wealthy families in America generally goes through four steps:

  1. Control resources, technology, channels, or scale in new industries;
  2. Place personal wealth into structures such as companies, stocks, and trusts;
  3. Allow assets to continue growing through inheritance, reinvestment, and family governance;
  4. Use universities, foundations, boards, political donations, and social relationships to convert economic capital into more enduring institutional capital.

The Rockefeller family is a typical example of this chain. In 1870, John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil, and in 1882 he consolidated assets across regions through a trust. In 1911, an antitrust lawsuit led to the breakup of Standard Oil, but dismantling a monopoly did not mean scattering the shareholders’ equity, investment returns, business expertise, and social relationships. Afterwards, the family again transformed part of its wealth into long-term influence through foundations, educational and research institutions. Rockefeller Archive Center: John D. Rockefeller, 1839–1937

The United States is not without concerns about wealth concentration. The federal estate tax began in 1916, and one of its historical purposes was to limit excessive wealth concentration and observe intergenerational transfers. But the existence of the estate tax precisely demonstrates that the United States allows private wealth to be passed down within certain boundaries, while using taxation and antitrust measures to suppress the most extreme concentrations, rather than institutionally abolishing private family capital. IRS: Estate Tax Returns Revisited, 1916–1931

The key to American dynastic wealth, therefore, is not “having many children,” but rather the ability of wealth to be privatized, incorporated, and inherited, while continuously being reinforced by schools, institutions, and social networks outside the family. Population size only determines how many inheritance nodes exist; property rights and organizations determine whether these nodes can become enduring sources of power.

Even if birth restrictions are lifted, the population structure will not reverse immediately

China’s birth policy did not jump directly from “strict restrictions” to “full liberalization.” In 2016, the comprehensive two-child policy was implemented. In 2021, the three-child policy was further implemented, with the elimination of restrictive measures such as social maintenance fees and the removal of penalty provisions that no longer fit the new policy. The policy direction has changed, but the population age structure that has already formed will not be rearranged overnight along with the legal text.National Health Commission: Comprehensive Two-Child PolicyNPC: Explanation of Legislative Amendments Related to the Three-Child Birth Policy

Data released by the National Bureau of Statistics for 2025 laid this lag bare: at year-end, the total population stood at 1.40489 billion, with 7.92 million births and 11.31 million deaths over the year, a net decrease of 3.39 million; the population aged 60 and above reached 323.38 million (23.0%), and those aged 65 and above numbered 223.65 million; the 16–59 age group still comprised 851.36 million people, with a total of 725.04 million employed nationwide at year-end. National Bureau of Statistics: 2025 Statistical Communiqué on National Economic and Social Development

These sets of numbers are not in conflict with each other. They describe the current positions of people born in different years: the elderly population is the result of birth rates from decades ago, today’s working-age population is the stock of past birth peaks, and today’s newborns will not become part of the large-scale labor force until twenty years from now.

There will be a shortage of people in the future, and even today some may not be able to find their place

There are at least three clocks here:

Clock Pace of Change What It Alters Today’s Misalignment
The Demographic Clock Slowest, usually measured in decades Long-term supply of working-age population Children being born today cannot solve the immediate employment problem
The Industry Clock A few years Number of jobs and skill requirements Automation and upgrades change “what kind of people are needed”
The Employment Clock Nearly instantaneous Whether an individual can find a matching job Certain types of workers are in oversupply, while caregiving and technology positions are short-staffed

The population clock ticks the slowest — children born today will not significantly enter the labor market until the 2040s; the industrial clock ticks faster — automation, artificial intelligence, and industrial upgrading can change the skill requirements of jobs within just a few years; the employment clock is almost instantaneous — those with mismatched education, age, location, and skills may find themselves out of place immediately. “Too much labor,” more accurately stated, means too many of certain people relative to current effective demand.

This is why aging and employment pressure can coexist: the future working-age population will shrink, yet today’s existing labor force may not be able to transition to new jobs in time. Changes in total population cannot solve skill mismatches; nor can having more children address next quarter’s job shortages.

The truly difficult challenge is not drawing up another demographic target sheet, but reconnecting the three clocks. Fertility support must reduce the costs of housing, education, childcare, and caregiving so that families dare to plan for the future; industrial policy must create demand that can absorb workers, rather than merely boosting the productivity of a privileged few; education and training must enable people to transition from shrinking industries into growing ones; and eldercare and caregiving need to shift from being hidden responsibilities borne within the family to becoming formal services that can be employed and afforded.

In hindsight, the family planning policy was a development trade-off constrained by history: it traded a lower population growth rate for a resource buffer, while also postponing part of the structural costs to a later time. It thinned out the lateral kinship networks of many families, but it did not determine whether China could form plutocratic families. What always determines whether wealth can be passed down across generations is property rights and organizations.

The same holds true today. What a country truly lacks is not just future children, but positions that can provide today’s people with income, skills, and dignity. Otherwise, young people will be asked to have children to address the labor shortage twenty years from now, while seeing no reason to stay in the current job market before their eyes.

References

  • National Bureau of Statistics: Coordinating Population Development Strategy to Achieve Balanced Population Development
  • National Health Commission: Reply to Suggestion No. 4776 of the Fifth Session of the 12th National People’s Congress
  • National Health Commission: Vice Director of the National Health and Family Planning Commission Answers Reporters’ Questions on Implementing the Universal Two-Child Policy
  • Population and Family Planning Law as Amended in 2015
  • Historical Versions of the Beijing Population and Family Planning Regulations
  • National People’s Congress: Explanation on the Draft Amendment to the Population and Family Planning Law
  • Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference: The Socialist Transformation of Capitalist Industry and Commerce
  • Rockefeller Archive Center: John D. Rockefeller, 1839–1937
  • Internal Revenue Service: Estate Tax Returns Revisited, 1916–1931
  • National Bureau of Statistics: Statistical Communiqué of the People’s Republic of China on the 2025 National Economic and Social Development
