$blog-writer Why did China have the one-child policy, and the one-child policy particularly restricted public officials. To a certain extent, did it limit the formation of large family clans during the early years of the founding of the People’s Republic? The United States has many plutocratic families — how were they formed? Now that the one-child policy has been relaxed, the population structure faces two problems: aging combined with industrial upgrading. On one hand, there will not be enough people in the future; on the other hand, there is currently a surplus of labor, and the job market cannot absorb it.

item.title: Stainless Steel Is Not Just About 304; Standards Are the Easiest Point of Confusion in Online Purchase Disputes
item.description:
A Zhihu topic discussion went like this: someone bought a stainless steel item on Taobao that seemed to not match its advertised specifications, and got into a back-and-forth dispute with the seller. In the comment section, several familiar suggestions quickly appeared: buy from a brand, go to JD.com, or go to Pinduoduo—at least those platforms have customer service; others provided a list of standard numbers, saying don’t just ask about 304 and 316, ask about GB 4806.9 and GB/T 29601.

Half of this kind of advice is correct, but the other half muddles together four different things into one answer: steel grade, food-contact safety, product performance standards, and the path to liability when disputes arise. A genuinely useful buying approach isn’t memorizing some “customer service code phrase,” but knowing exactly what question each standard is answering.

Review the Comments First: The Direction is Right, But the Wording is Inaccurate

Statement in the comment Verification result More accurate understanding
304 and 316 are U.S. standards, so you can label them however you want without breaking the law Does not hold 304 and 316 are common steel grade designations or generic names; the grade must match the actual material, and no exemption from proper labeling exists simply because it comes from a certain numbering system
You should buy GB 4806.9-2016 Already outdated GB 4806.9-2023 came into force on September 6, 2024, and replaces the 2016 version
You should buy GB/T 29601-2025 Only half right The 2025 version has been released, but as of September 1, 2026, it has not yet come into force; the current version is still GB/T 29601-2013, and the 2025 version takes effect on November 1, 2026
Just asking customer service for the standard number is enough Not enough You also need to verify the specific material, food contact declaration, product category, manufacturer, and the corresponding certificate of conformity

304 and 316 are not themselves synonyms for “food grade.” In the standard interpretation for household stainless steel sinks issued by the State Administration for Market Regulation, SUS304 is mapped to 06Cr19Ni10 and SUS316 is mapped to 06Cr17Ni12Mo2, while other stainless steel materials such as 201 and 430 are also listed. What these designations first answer is “what material this is, and roughly where its composition and properties sit,” not “this product has already passed all food-contact safety requirements.”

Therefore, treating “304 and 316 are American standards” as a legal conclusion that allows them to be “used arbitrarily” is unfounded. 304 and 316 are better understood as common steel grade designations or generic names; in the context of domestic regulation, consumers should be able to see the material type and composition, or Chinese standard designations and unified numerical codes, such as 06Cr19Ni10 and S30408. Using only vague terms like “high-quality stainless steel” or “premium stainless steel” does not allow consumers to know what they are actually purchasing.

“National Standard” Is Not a Type of Steel, but Several Different Requirements

If the product will come into contact with food, the first thing to look at is the mandatory safety requirements for metal materials intended for food contact. The current GB 4806.9-2023 applies to metal materials and products intended for food contact, and covers not only the alloy grade but also issues such as raw materials, surface condition, migration of metallic elements, and labeling. It addresses whether an item can be manufactured and used in compliance with food-contact product requirements.

GB/T 29601, on the other hand, is the product standard for “Stainless Steel Hollowware,” which is a recommended national standard. It addresses the specific quality and performance requirements for hollowware-type products. It is not a one-size-fits-all standard for all stainless steel products: items such as thermos cups, sinks, and knives each have their own corresponding product standards. You should look up the standard that applies to whatever specific product you are buying.

The relationship between the two can be simply expressed as:

Material specifications; GB 4806.9 sets out the safety baseline for food contact; specific product standards describe the performance requirements of containers or other products. All three are listed on the page, which does not mean that the actual goods received will necessarily match the page.

This is also why having “written GB 4806.9-2023” still does not constitute a test report. The standard number only indicates which set of rules the seller claims to follow; it cannot independently prove that the actual material, production batch, and tested sample of this product are consistent with one another. Conversely, you cannot immediately conclude that a product must be counterfeit just because it does not list all relevant standard numbers in a prominent location; you also need to consider the label, instructions, packaging, product category, and actual test results.

Why Brands and Platforms Change the Dispute Experience

The comments say to buy from a brand, JD.com, or Pinduoduo. What people actually value may not be that a certain platform can turn steel into better steel, but three more practical things: the seller’s identity is easier to verify, transaction records are easier to preserve, and there is an entry point to continue submitting evidence after a dispute arises.

The E-Commerce Law requires operators to disclose product information in a comprehensive, truthful, accurate, and timely manner. It also requires platforms to verify the identity information of registered operators and to preserve product and transaction information. For businesses that the platform marks as self-operated, the platform must clearly distinguish them from the businesses of other operators on the platform, and must bear the civil liability of a product seller or service provider for self-operated business. As for ordinary platform stores, the platform does not automatically become a guarantor of product quality simply by providing the webpage; only under specific conditions—such as knowing or having reason to know of an infringement of consumer rights and interests while failing to take necessary measures—will it be subject to corresponding liability determination.

Therefore, brands, flagship stores, self-operated channels, and large platforms are ways to reduce information asymmetry and the cost of providing evidence—not proof that “there will absolutely never be counterfeit goods.” Taobao, JD.com, and Pinduoduo should not be simply ranked into safety tiers either: within the same platform there are different sellers, and the same brand may have different channels, different batches, and different products.

When Asking Customer Service, Don’t Just Ask “Is This the Standard”

You can break the question down into the following four sentences and ask the other party to reply explicitly in the platform chat:

  1. For the metal parts that come into direct contact with food, what are the specific material types and the corresponding Chinese standard grades or unified digital codes? Please do not simply reply with “food-grade” or “304”.
  2. Is this product manufactured in compliance with GB 4806.9-2023? Can you provide the corresponding declaration of conformity and product qualification certificate? If a test report is available, do the model, batch, and sample in the report correspond to this product?
  3. What product standards apply to this category? If it is a common stainless steel utensil, as of September 1, 2026, please distinguish between the current GB/T 29601-2013 and the issued-but-not-yet-implemented GB/T 29601-2025.
  4. What are the manufacturer’s name, address, contact information, product model, and date of manufacture? Can the packaging and product listing be matched with one another?

If customer service can clearly explain each of these details item by item, consumers will have material they can compare and keep on record; if they merely keep repeating “don’t worry, it’s food-grade 304,” this doesn’t prove the merchant has committed fraud, but at least it shows the consumer still hasn’t completed the verification. Taking screenshots of the product page, standard number, and material commitments before placing an order is often more useful than arguing from memory after receiving the goods.

Already suspecting you bought a fake, first preserve the evidence chain

First, for products that come into contact with food, suspend their use until the material and safety have been clarified. Do not continue using them to hold food just because they look like stainless steel. Also, “not being 304” should not be directly equated with “definitely toxic”: the grade, food-contact compliance, and actual migration risk are not the same judgment; what is truly needed is evidence corresponding to the specific product and batch.

Second, preserve the product detail pages, promotional images, customer service chats, orders, payments, logistics, outer packaging, labels, and product photos. Do not discard the packaging and labels just to facilitate a return, and try not to move communications off the platform. The online shopping tips issued by the market regulation authorities also list these records as evidence for consumer rights protection.

Third, submit a clear issue through the platform’s after-sales service: what material was advertised, what label was received, what proof has the merchant provided, and where exactly the discrepancies lie. If negotiation fails, then file a complaint with the platform, the market regulatory department at the merchant’s actual place of business, or a consumer organization. When the specific composition needs to be confirmed, a qualified inspection or regulatory sampling is more likely to turn “it doesn’t look right” into a fact that can be acted upon.

Standards Do Not Give Counterfeits the Green Light

“The manufacturers know these labels aren’t illegal, so they do it this way” is an understandable suspicion, but at present this statement is still an inference about subjective intent and cannot be directly drawn from a single product label or a customer service conversation. In reality, there are at least three possibilities: the label and materials are both compliant, it’s just that consumers don’t understand them; the company’s labeling is vague or incomplete; or the company knowingly violates the rules and still engages in false advertising. Each requires different evidence.

What is certain is that the labeling of food-related products must be clear, truthful, and accurate, and must not deceive or mislead consumers. Operators must also disclose product information truthfully, comprehensively, and accurately. The standard does not turn “304” into a disclaimer word, nor does it turn “GB 4806.9” into a quality talisman. What it truly provides is a verification path: first ask about the intended use, then check the current standard; next, look at the specific grade, material composition, manufacturer, and certificate of conformity; and finally, treat the platform’s after-sales service and regulatory complaints as an extension of the evidence chain.

When buying stainless steel, the most worthwhile questions to ask are not “Is there a standard number that sounds tough?” but rather: “Does this standard correspond to my product? Are this piece of material and the label referring to the same thing? If they don’t match, can I leave sufficient evidence on the platform?” These questions come closer to real consumer protection than simply memorizing 304 or 316.

References

  • GB 4806.9-2023 Standard Details, Zhejiang Provincial Administration for Market Regulation Standards Online (verified on 2026-09-01)
  • GB/T 29601-2025, National Standards Information Public Service Platform (verified on 2026-09-01)
  • GB/T 29601-2013, National Standards Information Public Service Platform (verified on 2026-09-01)
  • GB/T 20878-2024, National Standards Information Public Service Platform (verified on 2026-09-01)
  • Interim Measures for the Supervision and Administration of Food-Related Product Quality and Safety, SAMR
  • Consumer Tips for Tableware and Other Products During the Spring Festival, SAMR
  • Food-Related Product Selection and Usage Tips — Metal and Enamel Categories, SAMR
  • Interpretation of the National Standard “Household Stainless Steel Sinks”, SAMR
  • Stainless Steel Kitchenware Product Knowledge and Consumer Tips, Jinan Municipal Administration for Market Regulation
  • E-Commerce Law of the People’s Republic of China, SAMR
  • Guizhou Issues “Double 11” Online Shopping Consumer Tips, SAMR
  • What Kind of Vacuum Flask Is Safe and Insulating, SAMR
写作附记

Original Prompt

A topic seen on $blog-writer Zhihu: someone bought fake stainless steel on Taobao, went back and forth arguing, and commenters below discussed buying from brands, JD.com, or Pinduoduo—at least customer service handles these issues. Some also mentioned regulation, and the most useful comment was this: 304 and 316 are American standards that can be labeled arbitrarily without breaking the law; to buy according to Chinese national standards, look for GB 4806.9-2016 and GB/T 29601-2025, just ask customer service directly whether the product complies with these standards—the latest standard is already GB 4806.9-2023. It’s essentially the case that manufacturers know these labels aren’t illegal, which is why they do this. Check the reasonableness first, then write the corresponding article.

This article separates several claims from the comments: 304/316 are material grades, GB 4806.9-2023 is the current safety standard for metals in food contact applications, and GB/T 29601-2025 is a recommended standard for tableware that has been published but, as of the date of this article, has not yet come into effect. The article does not characterize paraphrased Zhihu comments—without specific products, reports, or orders—as the illegal conduct of any particular merchant, nor does it present any brand or platform as an absolute guarantee.

item.title: Expansion Is Already on the Way, So Why Won't Memory Get Cheaper Anytime Soon
item.description:
The pressure from consumer electronics is showing up in end-device pricing and shipment expectations. Both IDC and Gartner’s models suggest that rising memory costs will push up the average selling price of PCs and smartphones while reducing shipment volumes. The specific figures and models differ between the two, so they cannot be combined into a single unified conclusion. This naturally raises a question: aren’t memory manufacturers all expanding capacity? When will memory prices come down?

As of August 12, 2026, the answer based on publicly available information is not straightforward: The second half of 2026 looks more like a slowdown in price increases rather than a broad-based price decline; the second half of 2027 is one of the earliest windows in which NAND Flash supply and demand may gradually ease, but it is neither a DRAM price-cut schedule nor a guarantee for retail prices of PCs, smartphones, and SSDs.

The scope of discussion here is limited to DRAM, NAND Flash, and the PCs, phones, and storage products whose costs are pulled by them. It should not be extrapolated into “when will all semiconductors drop in price”: mature process nodes, logic foundry, MCUs, analog chips, and advanced packaging each have their own supply and demand cycles.

“Capacity Expansion” is not a number that can be directly added

What most commonly appears in the news are investment amounts, factory groundbreaking ceremonies, cleanroom floor space, or the overall production capacity of a wafer fab. But what consumers end up buying are memory modules, flash chips, and modules that have gone through manufacturing, yield ramp-up, packaging and testing, and product allocation. At least three different layers of supply stand in between.

Layer What It Describes Why It Does Not Directly Translate to Consumer-Level Price Drops
Wafer or Clean Room Capacity The physical foundation of fabs and manufacturing capability It may be foundry-only or not yet in production; it is not equivalent to finished DRAM or NAND output
Bit Output from Process Migration The increase in storage bits producible on the same wafer It requires yield, product mix, and market deployment to align; fab count alone is not sufficient
Effective Sellable Supply Qualifiable finished products allocable to PCs, phones, and SSDs Allocation can be shifted by priority demand such as HBM, high-capacity DDR5, and enterprise-grade products

TSMC is a good counterexample. Its 12-inch equivalent capacity for 2025 exceeds 17 million wafers, and its capital expenditure for 2026 is projected at 52 to 56 billion USD, with a focus on 2nm, 3nm, specialty processes, and advanced packaging. This is a company-wide wafer metric and cannot be used to calculate the increase in DRAM or NAND output, let alone serve as evidence that memory prices for phones and PCs will fall. The semiconductor industry does not have a unified “total capacity table,” nor does a single unified price curve exist.

Samsung’s materials likewise remind us not to mistake long-range construction plans for near-term supply. The company stated in 2023 that, under its planning at the time, cleanroom capacity by 2027 would reach 7.3 times that of 2021; this is a long-term foundry cleanroom goal, not the number of wafers already in production and available for memory. By 2026, Samsung had additionally announced HBM4 mass production and a supply collaboration with AMD, which can be read as a sign that high-end AI memory is still receiving prioritized advancement, but this is not a complete capacity allocation ranking.

These projects are really about memory, and their timelines are much longer than just “breaking ground.” Micron’s new Singapore NAND fab, announced in January 2026, is scheduled to begin wafer output in the second half of 2028; HBM advanced packaging at the same site is expected to start generating meaningful supply in 2027. Among its U.S. DRAM expansions, the first Idaho fab is expected to produce its first wafer by mid-2027, the second fab by the end of 2028, and the New York project comes even later. A first wafer does not equal mature yields and shippable finished products, and the product mix can be adjusted according to the market; none of these milestones can be equated with new sellable supply of consumer-grade memory in the current quarter.

SK Hynix has announced the construction of the M15X DRAM fab in Cheongju and completed the M16 fab. However, the public fact sheet does not provide current monthly wafer output figures that can be aggregated horizontally with other manufacturers. Rather than piecing together a seemingly precise “capacity ranking of each company,” it is better to acknowledge that the units, timing points, and product calibers publicly disclosed by different companies are inconsistent, and forcing them to be aggregated would only produce erroneous conclusions.

Where Supply Went Is More Important Than Total Supply

What makes this round special is not just the “limited supply,” but the shift in where new resources are being directed. IDC forecasts that DRAM and NAND supply growth in 2026 will be 16% and 17% respectively, while also noting that capacity is being prioritized for AI data center products such as HBM and high-capacity DDR5. Samsung’s mass production of HBM4, along with Micron’s decision to place HBM packaging at earlier nodes at its Singapore facility, also corroborate this phenomenon.

This means that even if the total bit output increases, how much incremental supply consumer-grade conventional DRAM and NAND can obtain still depends on the manufacturers’ product mix and profit considerations. The high-end memory and advanced packaging capabilities required for servers are not fully interchangeable with consumer-grade chips; therefore, “significant AI-related investment” cannot be automatically translated into “256GB SSDs will be cheaper.”

Institutional Assessment: First Distinguish Among the Three Kinds of “Price Reductions”

Market discussions often combine three different signals into a single term: contract price decline, easing supply-demand in the industry, and a decrease in end retail prices. These are three signals that need to be observed separately, and their transmission timing and sequence may not be consistent, nor necessarily occur in the same quarter.

TrendForce’s forecast for Q3 2026 shows that conventional DRAM contract prices will still rise 13% to 18% quarter-over-quarter, while NAND Flash contract prices will increase 10% to 15% quarter-over-quarter. This already falls within a “narrowing increase” context, yet it is still an increase rather than a decrease; moreover, contract prices represent the quarterly settlement benchmark between upstream buyers and sellers, and are not equivalent to retail shelf prices.

Regarding longer-term supply and demand changes, TrendForce projects that NAND will still have a supply gap of 4% to 5% in 2026; with the combined effect of process migration, growth in bit output, and weak consumer electronics demand, the tight situation will gradually ease in the second half of 2027. This is the judgment closest to an inflection window in the available materials, but the key word is “gradual easing.” It cannot be used to derive that a certain brand’s SSD will drop in price on a particular day, nor can it be extended to conclude that DRAM will necessarily decline over the same period.

IDC’s timing assessment is more conservative: price acceleration will slow in the second half of 2026, but prices will still rise and remain elevated, with the baseline model not pointing to a return to 2025 levels. Its judgment on PCs is that the global average selling price of PCs in 2026 will rise by 17%, and even with memory capacity expansion over the next two years, prices are unlikely to return to 2025 levels. For mobile phones, IDC forecasts shipments will fall to 1.09 billion units in 2026, a 13.9% year-over-year decline, drop another 1.1% in 2027, and rebound by 5.5% in 2028 once memory supply normalizes. However, this mobile phone forecast also incorporates geopolitical factors and transportation costs, so the entire decline cannot be attributed to memory.

Gartner’s model presents another measure of pressure: it estimates that the combined price of DRAM and SSD will rise 130% by the end of 2026 compared with 2025, while PC and smartphone prices will increase by 17% and 13% respectively, with corresponding shipment volumes declining by 10.4% and 8.4%. These figures differ from the specific numbers later updated by IDC, and the two should be understood as scenario estimates from different institutions using different models, rather than precise numbers that can be pieced together into an “industry consensus.”

What Long-Term Contracts Lock In Is Supply Visibility, Not Five-Year Net Profit

If we push the question one step further: since these vendors have begun signing multi-year long-term agreements, can we calculate the minimum profit over the next five years based on this? The answer requires more restraint than “when will prices drop.” Public disclosures currently only support a very limited but important conclusion: Micron has disclosed minimum revenue under contracts; the other three have disclosed multi-year partnerships, orders, or capacity plans. None of them have publicly disclosed complete economic terms sufficient to calculate the minimum net profit over five years.

Company Publicly Disclosed LTAs / Multi-Year Arrangements Verifiable USD Floor Can 2026—2030 Minimum Net Profit Be Calculated From This
Micron 16 SCAs typically covering 2026—2030, automotive agreements typically three years; includes minimum purchase volumes and price bands Cumulative minimum contracted revenue from 14 signed SCAs is approximately $100 billion No; revenue floor is not net profit
SK Hynix Completed multi-year LTAs with approximately ten customers Not disclosed No
Samsung Electronics HBM customer POs already in place for 2026, with customers pursuing discussions for multi-year supply in 2027 and beyond Not disclosed No
TSMC Capacity planning jointly based on customer multi-year demand Not disclosed No; its logic foundry profits cannot substitute for memory contract profits

Micron is an exception, but only as far as “revenue.” Its management stated that 14 signed agreements have cumulative revenue of approximately $100 billion over the remaining period at contract minimum prices, with the agreements typically extending through the end of 2030; these agreements cover roughly 20% of DRAM shipments and one-third of NAND shipments over the same period. Large contracts typically include price ceilings and floors, and are take-or-pay. This disclosure takes a portion of demand and pricing out of the spot cycle, thereby increasing visibility into future revenue.

But it cannot derive that “Micron’s minimum net income over the next five years is X USD.” Net income also depends on revenue outside the contract, manufacturing costs, yield and product mix, depreciation, R&D and selling expenses, interest, taxes, and other items; the strong gross margin cited by management does not provide a substitutable lower bound on net margin. Dividing 100 billion USD by five and multiplying by the current quarter’s or historical profit margin merely disguises a cyclical peak as a contractual commitment.

SK hynix has confirmed multi-year LTAs with about ten customers; Samsung has confirmed that customers are driving multi-year supply discussions and that the HBM models mass-producible in 2026 have already received orders; TSMC is allocating capacity based on customers’ multi-year demand plans. These developments explain why vendors are more confident in investing, and why consumer electronics cannot simply wait for one additional production line; however, contract amounts, minimum purchase volumes, pricing terms, and costs have not been disclosed. Based on currently public information, only Micron can confirm partial guaranteed revenue of roughly $100 billion from its contracts; none of the four companies can have their five-year minimum net profit calculated from the disclosed materials.

This is not an evasion of valuation, but rather a delineation of one. Long-term contracts are sufficient to reduce part of the uncertainty in sales volume and price, yet they do not turn memory cycles, cost curves, or corporate operating expenses into fixed values. For the reader, it reinforces the original judgment: supply tightness is no longer determined solely by short-term spot quotations; however, any table that translates long-term contracts directly into a five-year “guaranteed profit” goes beyond the public data.

If we adopt the consensus expectations from institutions, we can obtain a valuation table

If one is careful not to confuse “digits” with “long-term guaranteed minima,” the analyst consensus averages compiled by FactSet can be used. The table below shows each company’s “net profit (Gewinn)” series as publicly verifiable in this round; U.S. dollar figures are in billions, rounded to one decimal place. Micron and TSMC were originally denominated in USD; SK Hynix was originally in EUR, and Samsung was originally in KRW — all converted at the European Central Bank reference rate of 23 July 2026 (1 EUR = 1.1392 USD; consequently 1 USD ≈ 1,472.7 KRW). The currency conversion is solely for uniform presentation and does not alter the original analyst forecasts.

Company (Fiscal Year End) 2026E 2027E 2028E 2029E 2030E Minimum Value in Disclosed Series
Micron (August) 83.4 175.4 192.5 211.1 300.9 83.4 (2026E)
SK Hynix (December) 171.2 229.6 255.1 348.9 533.6 171.2 (2026E)
Samsung Electronics (December) 207.0 294.4 295.5 — — 207.0 (2026E)
TSMC (December) 86.4 113.5 142.9 177.9 — 86.4 (2026E)

This table answers the question “What is the lowest net profit among the disclosed years in the brokerage average scenario?"—not “the pessimistic lower bound for the next five years,” and certainly not a contractual guarantee. Samsung’s publicly available consensus net profit estimate extends only through 2028, while TSMC’s extends only through 2029; no extrapolation is made for the blank entries. Micron’s 2026E refers to its fiscal year ending August 2026, and cannot be treated as exactly the same observation window as the other three companies’ calendar-year fiscal years.

Notably, the minimum of all four average expected series falls on 2026E. This reflects the current shared assumptions among analysts regarding AI memory demand, the high-end product mix, and industry supply constraints; it does not imply that the next five years will only trend upward. Insufficient coverage by long-term agreements or orders, a renewed weakening of consumer electronics demand, process and yield issues, competitive capacity expansion, and exchange rate fluctuations could all cause these numbers to be revised. They can serve as a thermometer for readers to observe how the market is pricing future earnings, but they cannot replace judgments based on contract terms or consumer-grade memory prices.

What Signals Should Consumers and Buyers Wait For

If the goal is to find a realistic basis for “whether one can wait for a better price,” the first things to observe are not the groundbreaking news of a new factory, but rather the changes at each of the three levels separately, rather than treating them as a fixed buying clock.

First, whether the contract prices settled quarterly by upstream manufacturers and major customers for DRAM and NAND shift from “narrowing increases” to quarter-over-quarter declines; second, whether the industry supply-demand balance moves from a shortfall to equilibrium or even looseness, particularly distinguishing between NAND and DRAM; third, whether the inventory, promotions, and configurations at OEMs and retail channels transmit upstream changes into actual transaction prices. Brands may absorb part of the cost, adjust capacity configurations, or delay price adjustments, so the transmission at the retail end may be slower and may also move out of sync with the first two types of signals.

Based on the available information, the supply-demand easing window for NAND is being pointed to the second half of 2027, while the contract price forecast for Q3 2026 still points upward. For DRAM, the existing materials do not give a credible and明确的 starting quarter for decline; for retail prices of mobile phones, PCs, or SSDs, there is even no verifiable specific date for price reductions. Stating these unknowns clearly is more useful than giving a seemingly tidy but unsupported timeline.

Weakening consumer electronics demand does cap the pace of further price spikes, but it is not a switch that determines prices on its own. The push for high-end AI memory, the bit-growth brought by process-node advances, the speed at which capacity expansions are realized, and manufacturers’ product allocation together determine the effective available supply. As of August 12, 2026, expansion is underway; for consumers, what is truly worth waiting for is not news of factory construction, but the moment supply begins to enter the regular market in the right products and the right quantities.

This article is based solely on publicly available information for industry observation and does not constitute procurement or investment advice.

item.title: Going to Nanjing on a Typhoon Day, Walking Into the Underground of a City
item.description:
There was a typhoon in Shanghai over the weekend. When we headed out in the morning, the wind and rain hadn’t yet reached the point where walking became difficult, so we stuck to our original plan and took the high-speed train to Nanjing for a day trip. The itinerary was arranged by my wife—there was no mission to check off a bunch of tourist spots; it was just a leisurely stroll.

The benefit of this arrangement is that the city reveals a bit of its own character.

The library in Nanjing left me with a rather good first impression. You didn’t need to swipe a card to get in, and there was no sense of “this place isn’t meant for you.” Dropping into a library by chance while traveling is a bit different from visiting a famous attraction: there’s no rush to take photos, and no set route to follow. When you sit down, the city suddenly shifts from being a place-name on a map to a place where people actually live their lives.

Dinner was a bit of a letdown. I had been looking forward to the roast duck, but when it was served I realized it wasn’t the crispy-skinned roast duck I had in mind. Not that it was bad—it’s just that taste is hard to explain; my expectations had already sat down at the table before the food did. I still find myself thinking more about the roast goose back in Shenzhen: the skin should be a bit crispier, the richness of the fat a bit more direct. It’s not a bad thing to eat something that doesn’t quite suit your taste when traveling—at the very least, you won’t keep building it up in your imagination afterward.

What surprised me the most was the way to get around downtown Nanjing. Near Xinjiekou, one subway exit follows another, and it feels like you can never quite finish walking through them. I later found out that this station has at least twenty-four numbered exits. There isn’t always a convenient crosswalk on the surface; to get to the opposite side, you often have to go down underground first and come back up from another exit.

At first it feels a bit strange, but after walking around a while it begins to seem reasonable. Above ground there are streams of traffic, streams of people, and intersections; underground, it feels like another layer of the city: malls, subways, passageways, and exits all connect with one another. You think you’re just crossing a street, but in reality you’re winding your way through a very large indoor system. This is especially true on rainy days, when the underground space feels like an umbrella the city has handed you.

Deji Plaza is also part of this system. Inside are the familiar luxury stores, and since I am not their target customer, walking through them feels a bit like window shopping. What left a deeper impression was the restroom that everyone keeps talking about inside the mall. Some say it cost tens of millions; I have no way to verify whether that’s true. But the fact that they turned a restroom into a destination worth a special visit shows, at the very least, that the mall knows how to give itself an entry point that people will talk about and spread.

This reminds me of Changsha’s IFC (International Finance Center). Whenever I look at the luxury floors there, I don’t see many people actually browsing seriously; everyone seems to just pass through on their way upstairs to eat. What really keeps people around in a mall isn’t necessarily the most expensive things. It might be a meal, a corner where it’s easy to sit down, or a restroom that people want to photograph and tell their friends about.

This trip to Nanjing didn’t involve any particularly dramatic projects: setting off against a typhoon, walking a bit, visiting a library, having a meal of Peking duck that wasn’t entirely satisfying, and shuttling back and forth underground. But after returning, the things I remember most clearly are precisely these details that weren’t featured at the top of any travel guide.

A city is sometimes remembered not by its landmarks. It hides itself in exit numbers, in a stretch of pedestrian tunnel, and in places where you never intended to stop.

References

  • Public Reply from Nanjing Municipal Government on Exit 24 of Xinjiekou Subway Station, verified on 2026-08-11.
